questions.subject: GERMAN
questions.topic: The sharp s after a consonant before a vowel
questions.learningObjective: apply the post-1996 rule for the sharp s before a vowel and after a consonant
questions.stem: A learner is looking at an old printed notice that ends a word with a symbol that no longer appears in ordinary German. Which modern spelling of that word does the German orthography use instead?

options.misconception: keeps the old spelling of the sharp s that the reform of 1996 replaced before a consonant
puts the u in front of the sharp s, which produces a different sound from the one the word is meant to have
leaves out a letter the word needs in order to carry the long u of the syllable

questions.explanation: The rule that the reform of 1996 settled is the position of the sharp s. In front of a vowel, and after a long vowel, a double s is written, so Schluss and Fuss and dass. Behind a consonant the sign was dropped, so the old spellings Schluß, Fuß and daß went out of use. What remains is the rule that a word keeps the sharp s only where the sound after it is voiceless, as in die Straße, which is why one word can have ß and the next ss without either being an error.
questions.hint: Ask what sound follows the s, and whether a vowel or a consonant comes after it.

keeps the capital that the rules before 1996 made compulsory for an adverb made out of a day

questions.learningObjective: apply the post-1996 rule that abolished the comma before an infinitive clause

splits the compound into two separate words, which no rule of the reform permits

The reform made the capital optional rather than compulsory, so the old spelling is still not wrong, and that is why both forms appear in print from the same year onwards.

gives the word that is standard in Germany and understood in Austria as a loan rather than as the everyday word

names a different plant in the German of both countries, and the two words are not interchangeable

names a wheel or a bicycle only in a compound such as Radsport, not the machine by itself
is a plain description of two wheels rather than a word for the everyday vehicle

keeps the sharp s in the middle of the word, which the country in question never does

das Tram in Germany and die Tram in Switzerland

Dürfen Sie das Fenster öffnen? / Können Sie das Fenster öffnen?

answer.exemplar: The two claims are both right about different words, and the difference is not how informal the word is. A dialect form is a word of one local spoken variety, is not written down, and would be marked by a speaker of Standard German from elsewhere, so the Bavarian word for a wooden tub is a dialect form and nobody would put it in a formal letter. A regional standard is the ordinary word of a country: it is taught, printed and used officially, so Sackerl in Austria and Marille in Austria belong to this class. A learner who meets a regional standard should learn it as the word of that country and keep using the shared word in a German text, because both are correct and the audience decides which one is expected.

After a short vowel a doubled s is required instead, as in das Wasser and der Fluss, and the old spellings Fluß and Schluß are no longer standard in Germany and Austria. A learner who has only met the old rule writes Fluß for a short vowel and Straße for a long one, which is the reverse of the modern rule in both directions.
questions.hint: Ask how long the vowel in front of the final s is, and which letter that length requires.

questions.topic: A final consonant written one way and said another
questions.learningObjective: recognise the voiceless reading of a final consonant from the spelling of the word
questions.stem: A learner is told that the last consonant of a German word is often said with a different sound from the way the letter is written. Which of the four words is the one that shows this?

options.misconception: ends in a consonant that is not one of the letters affected, so nothing is said voiceless
ends in a two-letter consonant, so it is not one of the single letters affected
is pronounced exactly as its final consonant is written, so it shows no change of that kind

questions.explanation: A final b, d, g, p, t or k is pronounced voiceless at the end of a German word, so the d of die Jagd is said as a t and the g of der Tag is said as a k. The spelling does not change, which is why a learner can read a word correctly and still pronounce it wrongly. A final l or r is not affected, and a two-letter consonant such as ch is not affected either, because the rule applies to a single letter standing in a single position. This is the reason that reading German silently does not by itself fix the pronunciation.
questions.hint: Ask whether the last letter is one of the six that lose their voicing, and whether it stands on its own.
